inference_claims: Store managers compensate with informal workarounds based on private data and instinct, which keeps knowledge siloed and inconsistent.
Reliance on tacit experience leaves new store managers exposed, so outcomes depend on individual tenure.

insights.claim: Promotional stockouts stem from a timing gap: replenishment receives the promo calendar too late to cover supplier lead times.
insights.quote: the promo calendar is built by marketing in January and replenishment only sees it two weeks before launch. By then the supplier lead time is already longer than the notice we have.

insights.claim: No function owns the promo planning gap, with planning, marketing, and supply chain each assuming someone else is responsible.
insights.quote: Nobody. Planning thinks marketing owns it, marketing thinks supply chain owns it.

insights.claim: Stockouts carry a material, unowned financial cost of about 4% of promo revenue.
insights.quote: We lost roughly 4 percent of promo revenue last year to stockouts and nobody was accountable for that number.

insights.claim: Store managers compensate with informal workarounds based on private data and instinct, which keeps knowledge siloed and inconsistent.
insights.quote: They keep a private spreadsheet of what usually sells out and they over-order by instinct.

insights.claim: Reliance on tacit experience leaves new store managers exposed, so outcomes depend on individual tenure.
insights.quote: It works for the experienced ones. The new managers just get burned.

insights.claim: The existing weekly cross-functional call is well attended and could be leveraged, but it currently happens too late to influence decisions.
insights.quote: Our weekly cross-functional call is actually good, people turn up. It just happens after the decisions are made.

inference_claims: Theatre utilisation is low at around 68 percent, partly because unused blocks are released too late to be reallocated.

insights.claim: Theatre slot allocation is driven by seniority rather than need or efficiency, and the approach has remained unchanged for fifteen years.
insights.quote: By seniority, mostly. The most senior surgeons pick their blocks and everyone else fills what's left. It hasn't changed in fifteen years.

insights.claim: Theatre utilisation is low at around 68 percent, partly because unused blocks are released too late to be reallocated.
insights.quote: We run at about 68 percent. Blocks get released only 24 hours ahead, which is too late for anyone else to use them.

insights.claim: Previous reform attempts failed due to political resistance from senior surgeons protecting their autonomy, not because of weak evidence.
insights.quote: Both times the proposal died in the clinical committee because senior surgeons felt it threatened their autonomy. The data was never the issue.

insights.claim: Utilisation data is not fully reliable because anaesthetics and nursing record start times inconsistently, creating discrepancies of up to twenty minutes per case.
insights.quote: Anaesthetics logs start time differently from nursing, so the two systems disagree by up to twenty minutes per case.

inference_claims: Product gaps are a minor churn driver; the main cause is failure to embed the product in customers' daily workflow.
Discounting does not reduce churn, suggesting price concessions are an ineffective retention lever.

insights.claim: Churn concentrates in months four to six, coinciding with the handoff from onboarding to a pooled support team and the loss of a named contact.
insights.quote: Most churn happens in months four to six, right after onboarding ends. We hand the account to a pooled support team and the customer loses their named contact.

insights.claim: Product gaps are a minor churn driver; the main cause is failure to embed the product in customers' daily workflow.

insights.claim: The VP's top recommended fix is extending onboarding ownership to month nine, but it is blocked by an unapproved budget for two additional hires.

inference_claims: Actual compliance approval takes more than twice the formal timeline, largely due to time spent chasing missing documents from incomplete submissions.

insights.claim: Actual compliance approval takes more than twice the formal timeline, largely due to time spent chasing missing documents from incomplete submissions.
insights.quote: Formally in six weeks. In practice it's closer to fourteen because product teams submit incomplete files and we spend weeks chasing missing documents.

insights.claim: Incomplete submissions stem from an outdated requirements checklist that no longer reflects current compliance expectations.
insights.quote: The checklist lives in a PDF from 2019 that nobody has updated, so teams don't know what we actually require now.

insights.claim: The bottleneck is process design, not capacity: there is no triage to separate low-risk changes from complex new products.
insights.quote: Headcount is fine. What we lack is a triage step, so a trivial fee change waits in the same queue as a new lending product.

insights.claim: Compliance acknowledges the business's perception of it as a blocker is valid regarding speed, but defends the substance of its reviews.
insights.quote: Yes, and frankly they have a point on timing, though not on substance.
